passages.t: It is God who has done this
passages.happening:
‘Then Job answered’ (verse 1). “How long will you torment me and crush me with your words? Ten times now you have reproached me; you shamelessly mistreat me” (verses 2-3). Even if he had gone astray, he says, his error would be his own business.

If they insist on using his disgrace against him, “then understand that it is God who has wronged me and drawn His net around me” (verse 6). He cries out that violence has been done, and gets no answer. God has blocked his road and darkened his paths, stripped him of his honor and taken the crown from his head. ‘He tears me down on every side until I am gone; He uproots my hope like a tree’ (verse 10).

“His anger burns against me, and He counts me among His enemies. His troops advance together; they construct a ramp against me and encamp around my tent” (verses 11-12).
passages.hearers:
Bildad has just drawn the wicked man's end in pictures taken from Job's own losses. Job's answer is the emotional summit of the debate. First he goes lower than ever before. Then, from that lowest place, he rises higher than at any point in the book.

Ten times is a way of saying again and again. Job will not accept that his suffering proves him guilty. If someone has done wrong in this case, he says, it is God.

The siege picture in verse 12 comes from ancient warfare. Armies built earthen ramps up to a city's walls to bring battering rams against them. Job feels that God has brought a whole army, ramp and camp, against a single tent.
passages.asks: Job would not let his friends call his suffering his own fault. Ask whether you have accepted blame for something that was not yours to carry. And ask whether you have laid blame on someone else that was not theirs.

passages.happening:
“He has removed my brothers from me; my acquaintances have abandoned me. My kinsmen have failed me, and my friends have forgotten me” (verses 13-14). His guests and servant girls treat him as a stranger. He calls his servant, and the servant does not answer, though he begs him.

“My breath is repulsive to my wife, and I am loathsome to my own family” (verse 17). Little boys mock him. His closest friends despise him, and those he loves have turned against him. ‘My skin and flesh cling to my bones; I have escaped by the skin of my teeth’ (verse 20).

“Have pity on me, my friends, have pity, for the hand of God has struck me. Why do you persecute me as God does? Will you never get enough of my flesh?” (verses 21-22).
passages.hearers:
The list of abandonments shows how much a man's identity depended on his household. Brothers, relatives, guests, servants, a wife, the children in the street and close friends formed the whole web of a man's life. Losing their respect meant losing his place in the world.

This is suffering as loneliness, and Scripture treats it as a real part of affliction. Job's hope, when it comes in verse 25, rises from inside this loneliness, not after it.

‘By the skin of my teeth’ (verse 20) is a proverbial phrase. Job means he has barely survived, with almost nothing left.

His plea in verse 21 is simple and terrible. He asks his friends for pity, because God has struck him. He does not want an argument. He wants them on his side.
passages.asks: Job's household turned away from him one by one. Ask who in your life has been left alone in illness or shame. And ask what pity, the kind Job begged for, would look like if you offered it this week.

passages.happening:
“I wish that my words were recorded and inscribed in a book, by an iron stylus on lead, or chiseled in stone forever” (verses 23-24).

Then: “But I know that my Redeemer lives, and in the end He will stand upon the earth. Even after my skin has been destroyed, yet in my flesh I will see God. I will see Him for myself; my eyes will behold Him, and not as a stranger. How my heart yearns within me!” (verses 25-27).

Job turns back to his friends with a warning. If they keep persecuting him, saying the root of the trouble lies in him, ‘then you should fear the sword yourselves, because wrath brings punishment by the sword, so that you may know there is a judgment’ (verse 29).
passages.hearers:
Lasting records in the ancient world were cut into stone. Kings carved inscriptions into cliff faces, among them the great rock inscription of the Persian king Darius I at Behistun, from around 520 BC. Writing with an iron stylus on lead may mean letters cut in lead, or letters cut in rock and filled with lead. Job wants his testimony kept in the most lasting form there is, so that his innocence could be read after his death. The book of Job itself has done that.

The key word of verse 25, Redeemer, go'el, comes from Israel's family law. The go'el was the nearest male relative, responsible for a family member in trouble. He bought back land a poor relative had been forced to sell, redeemed a relative sold as a slave, stood for a murdered kinsman's blood, and could marry a childless widow to carry on the family name, as Boaz did for Ruth. The same word is used of God as Israel's Redeemer. Job has just said that his brothers and kinsmen have abandoned him. With no human go'el left, he says he has one who lives.

In the end, acharon, can mean last in time, or be a title, the last one, the witness who stands up last in court and has the final word. Three times in verses 26 and 27 Job says that he himself will see God.
passages.later: The go'el was the nearest of kin in the law: ‘his nearest of kin may come and redeem what his brother has sold’ (Leviticus 25:25). And Isaiah gives the word to God himself: “Your Redeemer is the Holy One of Israel” (Isaiah 41:14).
passages.hard:
Who is Job's Redeemer, and does he expect to see God after death?

Both questions are debated. On the Redeemer's identity, many scholars think Job means God himself, appealing from God as accuser to God as defender, as in 16:19. Others think Job pictures a heavenly figure distinct from God who will stand up for him, like the witness or advocate of chapter 16. Christians have read the verse in the light of Christ, who is both God and kin to every human being, while recognizing that Job himself could not have known of Jesus. The New Testament does not quote these verses.

On the second question, the Hebrew of verses 26 and 27 is difficult. The phrase rendered ‘in my flesh’ (verse 26) can also be translated apart from the flesh, and the timing of ‘even after my skin has been destroyed’ (verse 26) is unclear. Some read the verses as hope of bodily resurrection. Others read them as hope of being cleared after death, without resurrection. Others read them as hope of seeing God before death, in this life, despite Job's wasting body, which is what happens in chapter 42. These notes take no side.

What is not in doubt is Job's certainty that he will see God for himself, and not as a stranger. It comes from a man abandoned by everyone, at the lowest point of his life.
passages.asks: Job had no one left to stand up for him, and he said his Redeemer lives. Ask what you know, as surely as Job did, even when you cannot see it. And ask who in your life needs someone to stand up for them as a go'el would.
